Sanatsujātīya
(‘that which is related to [the sage] Sanatsujāta’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata which has given us the great jewel of a scripture called the Bhagavadgītā, has also presented us with several other treatises of deep philosophical content. One such work, perhaps, next only to the Bhagavadgītā, is the Sanatsujātīya.
It forms a part of the Udyogaparva (chapters 42 to 46). The total number of verses is 145 (in four chapters) according to one version and 192 (in five chapters) according to another.
Being an important composition, it has drawn the attention of many commentators like शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820), Nīla-kaṇṭha (A. D. 1400), Sarvajña नारायण and वादिराज (A. D. 1480-1600).
When धृतराष्ट्र, the blind king, wants to listen to higher philosophical truths from विदुर, the latter excuses himself as unfit to impart the same. He then mentally prays to the great sage Sanatsujāta who appears instantly before him. At his request the sage gives a spiritual discourse to धृतराष्ट्र. It is this discourse that goes by the name Sanatsujātīya.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra questions Sanatsujāta thus: “I understand that you declare that there is no death at all. On the other hand I have heard that the देवस् (gods) and the असुरस् (demons) had approached प्रजापति to know how to overcome death (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad (Chapter 8.7-12). What then, is the truth?”
Sanatsujāta’s reply is spread over four chapters. It may be summarised as follows:
First Chapter (43 verses)
It is प्रमाद that is the real मृत्यु or death. प्रमाद means अज्ञान, इग्नोरन्चे of the real nature of the आत्मन्, the Self. This अज्ञान leads to अहङ्कार (egoism), काम (desire), krodha (anger), amārga (the wrong path), janma (birth and rebirth) and दुःख (suffering). This is how प्रमाद can be equated with death.
The only way to destroy this मृत्यु is by apramāda or ज्ञान (knowledge).
It is māyā which is anādi (beginning-less) that is responsible for प्रमाद. निष्कामकर्म (desireless action) gradually leads to ज्ञान by purifying the मिन्द्.
The last part of this chapter is devoted to a description of the jñāni or a man of realisation. His life is so pure that it is beyond all pairs of opposites like fame or blame.
Second Chapter (50 Verses)
Nature of ज्ञान is discussed in this chapter. It is certainly not intellectual scholarship of the वेदस् or other scriptures, but तपस् or austerity that leads to the purification of the मिन्द् in which ज्ञान as realisation of the आत्मन् (the true Self) arises.
Pure तपस् has to be free from twelve doṣas (defects) and seven nṛśaṁsas (cruel deeds). It has to be endowed with twelve guṇas (virtues).
Some of the doṣas are: krodha (anger), काम (lust), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion) and asūyā (jealousy).
The nṛśaṁsas include harming others, putting up with great disgrace for small gains, lack of wisdom and hatred of women.
The guṇas comprise the following: सत्य (truth), दम (self-control), adhyātmaśāstraśravaṇa (listening to the sacred scriptures), तितिक्षा (forbearance), दान (giving gifts), dhṛti (fortitude) and शम (internal peace).
Third Chapter (23 Verses)
This section is dedicated to a description of ज्ञानयोग. Knowledge of the Self or ब्रह्मन् cannot be obtained by hurrying up in one’s sādhana or practice. One can get it only by serving the गुरु or spiritual preceptor.
Vidyā or knowledge is secured in four stages: approaching a competent गुरु; increasing one’s power of understanding; ripening of the knowledge in course of time; listening to the śāstras and meditating upon them.
Fourth Chapter (29 verses)
This chapter, the last, gives a beautiful description of ब्रह्मन्, the object of ज्ञानयोग, by using a good number of expressions appearing in the उपनिषद्स्. There is a refrain of the line yoginaḥ tam prapaśyanti bhagavantaṁ sanātanam (‘The yogis see him, the Eternal Lord’).
Brahman is absolutely pure, free from all defects. It is the great light that illumines everything. All the gods including इन्द्र worship it. It is pūrṇa (full and perfect). Space, time and objects can never limit it. Even the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्) springs out of it. When this jīvātman realises his real nature that is ब्रह्मन्, in his own heart, he too shines in Brah-man. After this realisation he becomes free from all śoka (sorrow) and मोह (delusion).
Thus, this treatise which starts with an enquiry about death, ends in the description of इम्मोर्तलित्य्!

sāntapana
(‘[that which causes] great hardship’)
------------------------------------------
Prāyaścittas or expiations for sins is a common feature of practical हिन्दुइस्म्. One such is सान्तपन. It is prescribed for one who commits a sin that makes him lose his caste (jātibhraṁśakara), knowingly. It consists in subsisting on the पञ्चगव्य mixed with water in which कुश grass is soaked (See PAÑCAGAVYA for details.) on the first day and ड़स्तिन्ग् completely on the second day.
Two varieties of this expiation are also described: अतिसान्तपन and महासान्तपन.
In the latter, the sinner has to subsist on the six items (cow’s milk, curds, ghee, urine and dung as also water of कुश grass) individually for each day for six days and fast on the seventh.
In अतिसान्तपन, the duration is trebled; i.e., milk for three days and so on.
See also PRĀYAŚCITTA.

Sanātan Gosvāmin
(A. D. 1481-1558)
------------------------------------------
Sanātana Gosvāmin and Rūpa Gosvāmin (A. D. 1493-1568) were brothers. Along with their nephew, जीव Gosvāmin (d. A. D. 1609) they formed the three pillars of the चैतन्य Movement and the Acintyabhedābheda School of philosophy propagated by it.
Sanātana was a high officer in the court of a Muslim nawab. Once he was going to another place on some urgent work. When he was caught in a hurricane, he accidentally heard the conversation between a lady and her husband, who wanted to venture into the hurricane. This had miraculous effect on his मिन्द्. He forthwith resigned from his job and wanted to join चैतन्य महाप्रभु (A. D. 1485-1533). Though he was jailed by his employer, he managed to escape and approached चैतन्य to be accepted as a disciple, which he did.
Towards the end of his life he started living in वृन्दाबन्, the place closely associated with the boyhood of कृष्ण.
His works are: Gītāvalī, Vaiṣṇava-toṣiṇī, Bhāgavatāmṛta and Siddhāntasāra. Rasamayakalikā is another work but in Beṅgālī.

Śāntisūktas
------------------------------------------
When some unnatural or supernatural phenomena take place, foreboding some evil, remedial measures have to be undertaken. These are generally termed शान्तिस्. (See ŚĀNTIS for details.)
Even in some early Vedic mantras we find the idea of counteracting the evil effects of bad द्रेअम्स् (vide Ṛgveda 10.164.1-5; 8.47.16-18; 10.36.4; 10.37.4).
The Śāṅkhāyana-gṛhyasūtras (5.6, 7, 10, 11) prescribes the Ṛgvedic सूक्त (1.114 with 11 verses) for curing a person suffering from any disease.
In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (4.42) there are 37 mantras of śānti, of which 7 are from the Ṛgveda.
Several verses of the Atharvaveda (6.45.1; 6.46.1) also are prescribed for similar purposes.
The entire chapter 36 of the Śukla-यजुर्वेद Saṁhitā comprising 24 mantras is used as śānti during the प्रवर्ग्य rite (See PRAVARGYA.).
Such Vedic mantras are called Śānti-sūktas.

sandhyāvandana
(‘obeisance [to God] during dawn and dusk’)
------------------------------------------
The word सन्ध्या refers to that time when night passes into day and day passes into night. They are dawn and dusk. The ritual of offering one’s obeisance to God during these periods is known as सन्ध्या-vandana.
See UPANAYANA for details.

sandhyā
(‘junction [of day and night]’)
------------------------------------------
The religious rite to be performed at dawn and dusk by the dvijas (the ‘twice-born’, ब्राह्मणस्, kṣattriyas and vaiśyas) is called सन्ध्या or सन्ध्यावन्दन.
See UPANAYANA for details.
The word is also used to indicate the intervening period between two युगस्.
See also YUGAS.

Sāndīpani
------------------------------------------
Sāndīpani was a well-known ṛṣi who was running a गुरुकुल (forest academy), in Avantī, a sacred city of ancient India. कृष्ण and बलराम had their एदुचतिओन् under him. At the end of their training he requested them to get back his dead son who had been drowned in the sea. They did so after killing the demon पञ्चजन who had abducted him and visiting god यम, in whose world the boy was found.

Sanātanadharma
(‘the eternal religion’)
------------------------------------------
The word हिन्दुइस्म् for the religion it represents, is of very recent origin.
This religion had no particular name since the most ancient days, because there existed no other religion from which it had to be distinguished.
Some scholars of present-day हिन्दुइस्म् like to call it ‘Sanātanadharma.’
It is true that this word occurs in the Khānāpur plates of Mādhavavarma (vide Epigraphia Indica vol. 27, p. 312) assigned to the 6th century A. D. Other sources where it has been used are: Matsyapurāṇa 143.30-32; Bhāgavata 7.11.2 and Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.37-38.
However, in both these places the word does not refer to any specific religion, but, only to ancient practices of eternal value.
Yet, it is possible to apply this word to हिन्दुइस्म् since it reflects the true spirit of हिन्दुइस्म् correctly.
The expression धर्म (‘that which supports’) has three senses: God; any spiritual discipline that leads to God; duty.
‘Sanātana’ means the eternal.
Since the various sādhanas or spiritual disciplines taught by हिन्दुइस्म् have been proving their efficacy even today (as in the ancient period)—hence sanātana or eternal—ultimately leading to God, the Eternal Truth, it fully deserves the appellation ‘Sanātanadharma’.

sandhi
(‘agreement’)
------------------------------------------
According to the treatises on Hindu political science, a king can adopt six methods of policy. They are: सन्धि (agreement or peace-treaty), vigraha (taking a hostile attitude), आसन (indifference), yāna (preparing to attack the enemy), saṁśraya (taking shelter under a more powerful king) and dvaidhībhāva (adopting a dual policy).
A king is advised to enter into सन्धि (peace-treaty) with other kings, when—
—his own kingdom is beset with natural calamities;
—there are more powerful enemies whom he cannot cope with.
—He should thus wait for better days.
However, सन्धि is not advisable with kings who are equal or weaker in strength.
In सन्धि, the king can offer his army or treasury or cede a part of his territory to avoid total defeat or submission.
Several varieties of sandhis—from four up to sixteen—are described in works like Kāmandakīya (9.2-18) and Agni-purāṇa (240).
In Sanskrit grammar, the word सन्धि means coalescence of two letters coming into immediate contact. For instance, when the letter i comes in front of a, they coalesce into e, as in पर + īśa = pareśa.
In आयुर्वेद, it refers to the joints in limbs like the hands and the feet.

Santānagopāla
------------------------------------------
After completing his Vedic studies under his teacher सान्दीपनि, कृष्ण requested him to accept some gurudakṣiṇa. Then सान्दीपनि, knowing fully well of कृष्ण’s divinity, requested him to bring back his dead son alive, who had been drowned at the प्रभास, the famous पिल्ग्रिमगे centre on the sea-shore (in Gujarat near the Somanātha temple). कृष्ण did it by killing the demon पञ्चजन and bringing back the boy from the world of यम, the god of death.
This aspect of कृष्ण is known as सन्तानगोपाल. Iconographical works describe him as four-armed, carrying शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus), wearing yellow silken garments and adorned with peacock feathers. He is surrounded by cows, calves and cowherds.
See also SĀNDĪPANI.

Sanskrit Commission, Report of The.
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Saṁskṛta or the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे has always been held in high veneration by the Hindus, so much so that it has been christened as ‘Devabhāṣā’ (‘language of the gods’). The gods in हेअवेन् are very handsome. The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे is supremely elegant. The gods in हेअवेन् are eternally young and vigorous. The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे, even now, is eternally fresh and delightfully vibrant.
Like all things in life, Sanskrit too has had its glorious periods and spells of hibernation.
However, when India got political independence and its own government there was a new upsurge of the national spirit enlivening every aspect of Indian life. The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे which had held the Hindu nation together by its inspiring literature—whether sacred or secular—and the resultant culture, could no longer remain insulated from this new-found spirit.
Due to the patriotic zeal of some wise and sagacious leaders, both in the government and outside it, ‘The Sanskrit Commission’ was constituted by the Government of India on the 1st October 1956 with Dr. Suniti Kumar Chatterji an eminent scholar and linguist, as the chairman, and seven distinguished professors and savants as members.
The terms of reference were:
to undertake a survey of the existing facilities for Sanskrit एदुचतिओन् in Universities and non-University institutions and to make proposals for promoting the study of Sanskrit, including research; and
to examine the traditional system of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन् in order to find out what features from it could be usefully incorporated into the modern system.
The commission established its Secretariat at Poona (now Pune) on the 1st November 1956.
It issued a detailed questionnaire—both in English and in Sanskrit—comprising 33 major questions, each containing several subquestions (85 in all) covering all conceivable aspects of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन् and culture.
Apart from questions of a general nature, other aspects included in the questionnaire were:
Sanskrit Education—The Modern as well as the Traditional Systems;
Sanskrit Research;
Organisation and Administration of Sanskrit Studies and एदुचतिओन्.
Apart from distinguished scholars and professors of Sanskrit, the questionnaire was answered by a large number of persons from various walks of life who were deeply interested in the spread of the language. Nearly 1200 replies were received—about 470 being in Sanskrit—which were analysed, the analyses themselves running into 2653 typed pages.
The Commission took the trouble of collecting all the reports of various committees—eleven, to be more specific—appointed in the earlier years by several State governments on the same subject of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन् and studied them.
Members of the Commission toured the country extensively, visited most of the institutions connected with सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे and culture, and interviewed hundreds of interested persons to elicit their opinions.
The final Report running into 300 pages (size: ??? ) was submitted to the Government on 30th November 1957.
It consists of 12 chapters and 9 detailed appendices.
A Brief Summary of the Report
Chapter 1—Introduction
Apart from giving the details regarding the appointment of this Commission, reference is made to the work of two Educational Commissions and the Official Language Commission, all of which have touched upon the topic of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन्. Various Sanskrit Reorganisation Commissions appointed earlier by several State governments and Public Bodies have also been referred to.
Chapter 2—Historical Retrospect
This chapter gives a historical survey of Sanskrit studies in India, especially after the taking over of the country by the British. Whereas the old Pāṭhaśālā system, the traditional system, continued to survive, a new system, that of Colleges and Universities offering courses in Sanskrit, also developed side by side. The growth of institutions and activities on both these fronts over the last 150 years has been described here.
Chapter 3—The Present Situation
Activities of the Pāṭhaśālās, Secondary Schools, Colleges, Universities and Research Institutions as also various public movements devoted to the promotion of Sanskrit in some form or the other, have been reviewed here.
Chapter 4—Sanskrit and the Aspirations of Independent India
Realising the hopes and aspirations of the people of independent and resurgent India, this chapter discusses various topics, opening the case for Sanskrit. Some of them are: The importance of Sanskrit in Indian History and Culture; Sanskrit studies and Humanities; intrinsic worth and significance of Sanskrit literature for the full development of human personality; Sanskrit as a binding force both at the national and international levels; Sanskrit still a living force and a perennial source for the sustenance of the various regional languages; must be a part of general scheme of Indian एदुचतिओन्; should be accorded special treatment.
Chapter 5—Sanskrit Education
Sanskrit must be made one of the compulsory subjects in general एदुचतिओन् as a part of the curriculum in the Secondary Schools. The specialised study in the Pāṭhaśālās, in the modern Colleges and Universities should be better organised. As a part of this subject, the merits and drawbacks of the two systems are discussed as also how the two can be integrated.
It has been pointed out here how Sanskrit has to be treated as a complement to the higher study of modern Indian languages as also इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् and Indology.
Chapter 6—Teaching of Sanskrit
Methods of teaching Sanskrit, both ancient and modern, have been described here. The need to evolve suitable methods to teach it at different levels as also the necessary reforms in the system of examination have been suggested.
Chapter 7—Sanskrit Research
This chapter deals with Sanskrit Research in all its aspects. The topics discussed are as follows: significance of research for the growth of Sanskrit studies; research in the Universities; research scholarships and fellowships; adjudication of research theses; neglected subjects; research projects and research publications; seminars; Journals and Bibliographies; Research Institutions; All India Oriental Conference; a scheme for a Central Institute of Indology.
Chapter 8—Manuscripts
The question of Sanskrit Manuscripts has been tackled here—their search, collection, preservation, cataloguing, study and publication.
It is advised to set up a Central Manuscripts library.
Chapter 9—Sanskrit University
The question of setting up a Sanskrit University under the Central Government has been suggested as also a Central Board of Sanskrit Studies. States also can be encouraged to start similar Universities.
Chapter 10—Other Questions concerning Sanskrit
The following topics have been discussed in this section: Sanskrit and Religious एदुचतिओन्; the use of regional scripts for Sanskrit; Technical Termino-logy; Sanskrit as an Official Language of the Indian Union; State honours and patronage for Sanskrit Scholars; encou-ragement of Sanskrit through Maṭhas and temples; Vedapāṭha, Purāṇapāṭha and Paurohitya; technical disciplines like आयुर्वेद, ज्यौतिष and Śilpa; Sanskrit journals; popularisation of Sanskrit by various means; cheap editions of Sanskrit classics with translations in regional languages and English.
Chapter 11—Administration and Organisation of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन् and Research
The chief point that has been stressed is that the resources available through various Trusts and Endowments should be pooled and utilised for the promotion of Sanskrit.
Chapter 12—Conspectus and Recommendations
This section gives a brief summary of all the chapters followed by the Recommendations of the Commission.
Recommendations
The Recommendations are categorised under the following headings:
Sanskrit एदुचतिओन्;
Sanskrit Research;
Manuscripts;
Sanskrit Universities;
General;
Administration and Organisation.
1. Sanskrit Education
Sanskrit should be made a compulsory subject in the Secondary School Curriculum.
The three Language Formula should be amended as follows:
The मोथेर् Tongue (or the regional Language);
English;
Sanskrit (or a classical language as equivalent to Sanskrit).
The traditional Pāṭhaśālā system should be continued and preserved. It should be reorganised so as to include some modern subjects like the मोथेर्-tongue, English, General Science, Mathematics and Social Studies including Ancient Indian History and Culture.
The Pandit-Teachers should undergo a course of Teachers’ Training.
The remodelled Sanskrit High Schools or remodelled Pāṭhaśālās should lead to Sanskrit Colleges.
The Pandit-Teachers should be treated as equal to Graduate-Teachers in all respects.
In the College course leading up to the Graduate and Post-graduate Degrees there should be a provision for the study of Sanskrit under general as well as special subjects.
The Pāṭhaśālā system and the University systems should be retained as separate units, but gradually reformed to bring about greater measure of co- operation between them.
The Pāṭhaśālā Pandits should be employed to teach in the modern Colleges and the professors of the latter, in the Pāṭhaśālās, for the betterment of both the systems.
In the Degree and Post-graduate courses in Indian languages and Humanities, Sanskrit also should be one subject.
There should be an investigation into the methods of teaching Sanskrit to different categories of students, Indian and foreign.
The Pāṭhaśālā System has to be reformed by having Sanskrit as the medium of instruction, at least at the higher level, by introducing some subjects connected with Western thought and also by adding suitable extra-curricular activities. The examination system too needs drastic change. Oral examination of the old Śāstrārtha type (discussion and disputation on holy texts) should be a part of this new system of testing.
2. Sanskrit Research
Pāṭhaśālā Pandits too should be given the same facilities for Research in the Universities and Colleges.
High-grade Sanskrit Colleges with reputed Pandits on their staffs and well-equipped libraries should be recognised by the Universities for Research.
Critically editing and publishing rare manuscripts, starting of Research Journals in Sanskrit, opening of Research Departments for different Śāstras should be encouraged.
New Research Degrees like M.Litt., and D.Litt., should be introduced, both having viva voce tests. Attention should be paid to the many neglected fields demanding investigation by Research scholars. For instance: Vedic Rituals; Kalpasūtras; Śilpa (Sculpturing); ज्यौतिष (Astronomy); इचोनोग्रफ्य्; सङ्गीत (Music); Nāṭya (Dancing).
Greater facilities should be offered for the publication of the results of Research.
Manuscript libraries should be helped to bring out inventories and even publications of the rare works.
Non-official Sanskrit and Indological Institutes in the country should be brought under a comprehensive scheme of co- ordination and assisted with liberal grants. A Central Institute of Indology should be established, its core-section being devoted to Sanskrit.
The All-India Oriental Conference should be placed on a permanent basis with adequate financial assistance. It should be encouraged to invite scholars from other Asian Countries.
Suitable Prizes and Awards should be instituted for Sanskrit and Indological work.
3. Manuscripts
A Central Manuscripts Survey should be established with branches in different regions of the country. Its work should consist of Search, Survey, Collection, Safeguard, Cataloguing and Publication of the Manuscripts of Sanskrit and allied works.
The flow of manuscripts to foreign countries must be prevented by all means.
The Manuscript Libraries should give facilities to bona fide scholars and institutions to consult or borrow them.
4. Sanskrit Universities
Sanskrit Universities should be established in different areas to tone up and upgrade the traditional system of Sanskrit एदुचतिओन्. They should be the apex of the reorganised Pāṭhaśālā system. They should co-ordinate the working of the Pāṭhaśālās and Sanskrit Colleges. They should also function as Centres of Higher Learning and Research in Sanskrit.
All the Sanskrit Universities should be under the aegis of the Central Sanskrit Board, which must be a Statutory Body.
They should adopt Sanskrit medium at all levels, academic as well as non- academic. They should also produce books in Sanskrit embodying modern knowledge.
The Central Government should give a lead by establishing a centrally administered Sanskrit University, preferably in South India.
5. General
Sanskrit should be declared as an Additional Official Language.
Sanskrit should be officially used on all ceremonial occasions.
The infinite resources of Sanskrit literature like the Subhāṣitas should be utilised in Schools and Colleges for moral instruction.
Efforts should be made to teach a Uniform Standard Pronunciation of Sanskrit in all parts of the country, by employing qualified readers and teachers in areas where it is defective.
A comprehensive English-Sanskrit Dictionary of Scientific and Technical Terms should be compiled with the help of suitable experts.
Personnel recruited for the Indian Administrative and Foreign Services should be given opportunities through special courses of lectures to acquire adequate knowledge of Sanskrit thought and Indian Culture. Same policy can be adopted with regard to Indian students going abroad for higher studies.
Indian Embassies abroad must have Cultural Attachés possessing special competence in सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे, Literature and Culture.
Special attention should be made to preserve the Oral Tradition of the different वेदस् and their recensions as current in different parts of India; and especially the Sāmaveda. Tape-recordings can be made through the All India Radio 1.
Steps should be taken to train the required personnel for the exposition of इतिहास-Purāṇa. Pāṭhaśālās should introduce this also among their regular courses.
Gifted exponents of the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, the Gītā and the पुराणस् should be employed in Community Projects and National Extension Service Schemes to spread our culture among the masses.
Courses in Paurohitya and कर्म-kāṇḍa must be introduced in the Pāṭhaśālās.
Students of modern science and technology should be made familiar with the developments made in our ancient and medieval periods as per the standard works produced then.
Sanskrit should be popularised by adopting suitable measures. Some of them are: organisation of private classes; producing Popular Sanskrit booklets and selections with translations; celebration of days in commemoration of important Sanskrit writers and works; simplification of the methods of teaching Sanskrit; Sanskrit Literary Conferences; promotion of Sanskrit debates and original writings in Sanskrit; competitions in short stories, plays etc., in Sanskrit; musical recitals of Sanskrit classics; enacting Sanskrit Dramas.
Important Sanskrit texts which are no longer available, should be brought out in new editions by the Sahitya Akademi and other bodies.
6. Administration and Organisation
A number of Trusts and Endowments formed for the promotion of Sanskrit and allied purposes, now lying dormant, should be unearthed and be put to use to implement the various proposals given in this report.
A Central Sanskrit Board should be constituted and run on the lines of the University Grants Commission. It should concern itself mainly with Pāṭhaśālā एदुचतिओन् and privately organised Research Institutes in the country, by helping them in all possible manners. It should be vested with the authority to sanction the starting of Sanskrit Universities, to recognise them as statutory bodies, to give them suitable grants and generally to control their working. It should also co-operate with the Central Institute of Indology and the Central Manuscripts Survey.
A separate Ministry of Culture should be created in the Central Government and place all cultural affairs, (now spread over various departments or ministries) under it.
In the National Plans adopted by the Government, substantial amounts should be set apart for the development and promotion of Sanskrit on the lines set forth in this Report.
Epilogue
Since the dawn of political indepen-dence, several Commissions have been constituted both by the Central and the State Governments, concerning various issues facing the country. However, eventhough those Commissions with distinguished persons had given very valuable reports, not many of the recommendations have been implemented due to various factors including narrow political conside-rations. Unfortunately, most of the recommendations of this Report also have remained till now, on paper only. It needs true patriotism and statesmanship to appreciate and implement this magnificent Report, magnificent in the truest sense of the term.

śāntātīya-mantra
------------------------------------------
Several religious rites are performed while entering a newly-built होउसे. One such rite consists in making the होउसे śānta (peaceful to live in).
In a vessel of water a little rice, barley and a piece of gold are deposited. The priest goes round the होउसे three times from left to right, sprinkling the water on the होउसे with the śāntātīya mantras.
These are the fifteen mantras of the Ṛgveda (7.35.1-15). Since the word śam (peace) occurs several times in it, the मन्त्र itself is called śāntātīya. Several deities like इन्द्र, अग्नि, वरुण, पूषन्, भग, Aryamā, Dhātā, मित्र, वसुस्, रुद्र, सूर्य, अदिति and others are addressed to bestow peace.

Śani
------------------------------------------
Also called Śanaīścara (slow-moving), he is the seventh planet in the solar system.
The पुराणस् describe him as the son of सूर्य (Sun-god) and छाया (shadow goddess of सṁज्ञा, the true wife of सूर्य).
See NAVAGRAHAS.

santoṣa
(‘happiness’, ‘contentment’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras (2.32) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) describes सन्तोष as a part of the second step of योग, viz., नियम. It is defined as being contented with whatever one gets and not desiring for more.

Sanskrit Language
------------------------------------------
Origin
How a language—any language for the matter—could attain the present degree of sophistication and artistry, starting with a physical sign language and inarticulate babble is a mystery. It is a mystery that linguistics or phonetics or etymology or philology will never be able to solve!
Hinduism, however, has easily ‘solved’ the same by attributing the origin of all languages and sciences to God Himself! An interesting verse in an ancient work called Nandikeśvarakārikā declares that all the alphabets of the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे (and hence its grammar) have evolved out of the fourteen sounds made by Lord शिव through his डमरु (a small drum held in hand for making sounds), at the end of his cosmic dance.
Two Divisions
Though Sanskrit is called devabhāṣā—the language of the gods in heaven—in practice it is divided into two categories: the vaidika (Vedic) and the laukika (secular).
The वेदस्, the वेदाङ्गस्, the Upavedas and allied literature belong to the first group. All the other literature—from the itihāsas and पुराणस् right up to the modern Sanskrit literature—falls under the second group.
Vedic Literature
The earliest form of Sanskrit is that of the Ṛgveda.
According to the orthodox Hindu tradition, the entire body of the Vedic mantras (known as the Saṁhitās) was, originally, one mass. The sage कृष्ण द्वैपायन collected all these Vedic mantras and divided them into four groups as per the needs of sacrificial religion that was in vogue. Hence he was called वेदव्यास or व्यास. The four groups are: Ṛk, Yajus, Sāma and Atharva.
In course of time three more sections were gradually added to each of the four वेदस्. They are: ब्राह्मण, Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad.
(For details see VEDAS.)
Since the language of the वेदस् was archaic and the concepts were slowly becoming obsolescent, explanatory works became necessary. This resulted in the production of the six वेदाङ्गस् (limbs or subsidiary works). They are: शिक्षा (phonetics); व्याकरण (grammar); छन्दस् (prosody); निरुक्त (etymology); ज्यौतिष (astronomy); and, कल्प (practical method).
The four Upavedas (subsidiary वेदस्) viz., आयुर्वेद (health-sciences), धनुर्वेद (military science), Gāndharvaveda (science of मुसिच् and fine-arts) and अर्थ-śāstra (political science), are also sometimes included under the Vedic literature.
Various anukramaṇīs (works similar to an index) by authors such as शौनक and कात्यायन may also be classed under the Vedic literature.
Itihāsas and Purāṇas
The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि and the Mahābhārata of व्यास are known as the itihāsas. They contain ancient history as also plenty of religio-philosophical teachings. (See MAHĀBHĀRATA and RĀMĀYAṆA for details.)
The original basic material of the purāṇas—known as the Purāṇasaṁhitā—is as old as the वेदस्. Over the centuries, it gradually took the shape of the present पुराणस् and उपपुराणस् (each group containing eighteen works). (See PURĀṆAS.) Of these, the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Bhāga-vata are considered important.
Classical Sanskrit Literature
There was a gradual evolution of the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे from the archaic form of the Saṁhitās to the classical form, first through the ब्राह्मणस् and then through the epics. This vast and varied literature—both in content and in methodology—may now be summarised very briefly, as follows, arranging them in the English alphabetical order for convenience:
ALAṄKĀRASĀHITYA
It is the science of figure of speech. The Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत (200 B. C.) seems to be the earliest attempt at systematisation of poetics and dramaturgy. However, it is the well-known authors like Bhāmaha and दण्डिन् (6th century A. D.), Ānandavardhana (9th century A. D.) and Mammaṭa (11th century A. D.) who have contributed much to the development of this science. They were also responsible for the evolution of several sampradāyas or schools. (See ALAṄKĀRAŚĀSTRA.)
CAMPŪSĀHITYA
The campū is a composition in which there is a balanced combination of elegant prose and poetry, each embellishing the other. The Vedic ākhyānas might have laid the foundation to the later campū-literature.
The extant campūkāvyas belong to a period later than the 9th century A. D.
The following is a list of some of the more well-known works belonging to the campū literature:
Nalacampū of Trivikramabhaṭṭa; Campūrāmāyaṇa of भोज; Bhāgavatacampū by Abhinava कालिदास; Nīlakaṇṭha-vijayacampū of Nīlakaṇṭhadīkṣita; Viśva-guṇādarśacampū of Veṅkaṭādhvarin.
DARŚANAŚĀSTRAS
Philosophical schools are known as darśanas. The three heterodox schools (Cārvāka, Jaina and Bauddha) and the six orthodox schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, योग, Mīmāṁsā and Vedānta) as also several others have produced a voluminous literature in the form of sūtras and commentaries as also independent works.
It is the Brahmasūtras of बादरायण that has induced the maximum number of works.
GADYASĀHITYA
Earliest specimens of available prose go back to the era 3000 B. C., the age of the ब्राह्मणस्. Some of the उपनिषद्स् like the Chāndogya and the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka which are mostly in prose, go back to the same or an even earlier period.
In the sūtra-period also we come across prose in the form of the bhāṣyas or commentaries, some of which are quite elegant.
Literary prose must have been popular even in ancient times as mentioned by पतञ्जलि in his Mahābhāśya on the Aṣṭādhyāyī. They are the ākhyāyikās (stories) connected with Vāsavadatta, Sumanottara and others.
Depending on the style of writing, these prose works of the literary or classical type are divided into three groups: romances; popular tales; didactic fables.
The following works may be cited as examples of exquisite prose compositions: Daśakumāracarita of दण्डिन्; Kādambarī of बाण; Vāsavadatta of Subandhu; Tilakamañjarī of Dhanapāla; Gadya-cintāmaṇī of Oḍeyadeva.
KATHĀSĀHITYA
Sanskrit literature did not lag behind in the च्रेअतिओन् and propagation of stories. These stories were composed not only to reflect the nature of the contemporary society but also keep some great ideals before it.
Though the Vedic literature has stories in the form of ākhyānas, a serious attempt to compile a single volume, only of stories, is first found in the Bṛhatkathā in the Paiśācī language (a distorted version of Sanskrit). The Kathāsaritsāgara of Somadeva (11th century A. D.) is said to be a faithful translation of the Bṛhatkathā, the original of which is not available. The Bṛhatkathāmañjarī of Kṣemendra is an earlier attempt of the same type.
The other reputed works in this field are: Pañcatantra; Hitopadeśa; Vetālapañcaviṁśati; Vikramacarita and Śuka-saptati.
KĀVYASĀHITYA
Sanskrit literature is replete with kāvyās or poetical works of the highest quality. Starting with the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि as the earliest in the series—rightly called the Ādikāvya—there has been a galaxy of great poets and their works.
A very brief list of their names and some of their works may now be given;
KĀLIDĀSA (100 B. C.)
His poetical works are:
Kumārasambhava; Meghadūta; Raghu-vaṁśa; Ṛtusaṁhāra. Out of these, the Raghuvaṁśa has forty commentaries, the Sañjīvinī of Mallinātha being the best.
BHĀRAVI (450 A. D.)
Kirātārjunīya is his only work.
BHAṬṬI (5th century A. D.)
The Bhaṭṭikāvya (also known as Rāvaṇavadha) is his only work. Along with beautiful poetry, this work tries to make Sanskrit grammar easy for the students of that subject.
MĀGHA (A. D. 650)
His magnum opus and the only work is the Śiśupālavadha. It has eight commentaries out of which the Sandeha-viṣauṣadhi of वल्लभ (A. D. 940) is the best.
KṢEMENDRA (birth A. D. 1000)
Though nineteen works have been authored by him, mention may be made only of two poetical works: Rāmāyaṇa-mañjarī and Bhāratamañjarī. These are brief works but elegant.
ŚRĪHARṢA (12th century A. D.)
Out of his nine works, the Naiṣa-dhīyacarita dealing with the story of नल and दमयन्ती is considered the best.
He also wrote a highly polemical work on Advaita Vedānta called Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya, which reflects his erudition in that branch.
VEDĀNTA DEŚIKA(A. D. 1268-1369)
Though well-known as a prolific and scholarly writer on Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta, वेदान्त देशिक was also a great litterateur. Special mention should be made of his two works: Yādavābhyudaya and Haṁsasandeśa. The former contains the story of कृष्ण whereas the latter deals with that of राम and सीता, especially the sorrow of their separation.
NĀṬAKASĀHITYA
There is enough evidence—like the Saṁvādasūktas of the Ṛgveda—to prove that nāṭakas or dramas have existed since the most ancient times. The epics contain references to dances, dramas and theatres.
Bharata’s Naṭyaśāstra was the earliest treatise on dramaturgy.
Now, a list of well-known authors of nāṭakas and their works may be given:
BHĀSA
Earliest of the playwrights, भास might have lived during the period 500 to 400 B. C.
The dramas attributed to him are thirteen. Out of these mention may be made of the following: Pratimānāṭaka; Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa and Svapna-vāsavadatta.
KĀLIDĀSA (100 B. C.)
The three well-known dramas of कालिदास are: Mālavikāgnimitra; Vikramorvaśīya and Abhijñānaśākuntala.
The last has been considered the very best of all Sanskrit dramas. It is woven round the love between the king दुष्यन्त and the damsel शकुन्तला of divine beauty.
VIŚĀKHADATTA (7th century A. D.)
The Mudrārākṣasa is his magnum opus though two more dramas were composed by him.
How चाणक्य, the famous kingmaker and prime-minister of Candragupta Maurya won over Rākṣasa, the loyal premier of the Nandas and made him agree to be the prime-minister of Candragupta Maurya is the main theme of this work.
ŚŪDRAKA (5th century A. D.)
Śūdraka was perhaps a king. His only work is the Mṛcchakaṭikā (‘the mud-cart’). It is in ten acts and concerns mainly with the story of love between Vasantasenā (a prostitute of high culture) and Cārudatta a decent ब्राह्मण of noble character.
The drama is replete with प्राकृत् words also.
ŚRĪHARṢHA or HARṢAVARDHANA
The well-known emperor श्रीहर्ष or Harṣavardhana ruled at Sthāṇeśvara from A. D. 606 to 647. He was not only a great king but also an erudite author.
Ratnāvalī, Nāgānanda and Priya-darśikā are the three dramas authored by him.
BHAṬṬANĀRĀYAṆA (7th century A. D.)
The Veṇīsaṁhāra, a six-act play drawing its material from the Mahābhārata, is his only work. भीम’s character has been highlighted and represented ably.
BHAVABHŪTI (8th century A. D.)
He is considered almost equal to कालिदास as to the qualities of his dramas which are three: Mālatīmādhava; Mahāvīracarita and Uttararāmāyaṇa. He was also well-versed in the philosophical lore.
It is the last, in seven acts, that is more famous. It draws the story from the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa making some interesting changes in the original story to enhance the literary grace of the work.
Apart from these, there have been a few more less-known playwrights such as Murāri (8th century A. D.; Anarghya-rāghava), Rājaśekhara (circa A. D. 900; Bālarāmāyaṇa, Bālabhārata and Karpūra-mañjarī), Śaktibhadra (9th century A. D.; Āścaryacūdāmaṇī) and जयदेव (13th century A. D.; Prasannarāghava).
NIGHAṆṬU
Nighaṇṭu means a dictionary. The first ever dictionary in Sanskrit is the Nighaṇṭu, an ancient dictionary of Vedic words by an unknown author. The Nirukta of यास्क (800 B. C.) is a commentary on this Nighaṇṭu.
Till now 87 Sanskrit dictionaries have been traced and found to have existed. Only, very few of them have been printed so far.
The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsanam of Amara Siṁha (A. D. 500), more popularly known as the Amarakośa, is the best of Sanskrit dictionaries. It has 38 commentaries. (See AMARAKOŚA for details.)
Some of the other dictionaries worth mentioning are: Liṅgānuśāsana of Vyāḍi; Trikāṇḍakośa of Bhāguri; Śabdārṇava of वाचस्पति; Hārāvalī of Puruṣottamadeva; Abhidhānaratnamālā or Halāyudhakośa of हलायुध; Nānārthaśabdakośa or Medinīkośa of Medinīkara; Kalpadruma-कोश of Keśava; Śabdakalpadruma of Rādhākāntadeva; Vācaspatya of तारा-nātha-तर्क-वाचस्पति and Nānārthār-ṇavasaṅkṣepa of Keśavasvāmin.
PURĀṆASĀHITYA
Starting with the ākhyāyikās or stories carried over from the ancient (pre-Vedic) days, the purāṇa literature has now grown into a huge mass comprising the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and the eighteen (or even more) उपपुराणस्. (See PURĀṆAS for details.)
STOTRASĀHITYA
The stotrasāhitya or hymnal literature in Sanskrit is almost limitless. Great mystics and devotee-poets, in their moments of divine ecstasy have burst forth into innumerable hymns. These hymns are in various poetical metres and contain a variety of feelings and descriptions. They are addressed to the different deities of the Hindu pantheon such as शिव, देवी, विष्णु, गणपति, सुब्रह्मण्य and others.
Mention may now be made of a small fraction of these hymns. They are: Śivamahimnastotra of Puṣpadanta; Saundaryalaharī of शङ्कर; Mukunda-mālā of Kulaśekhara; Stotraratna of Yāmuna; Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta of लीलाशुक; Pādukāsahasra of वेदान्त देशिक; Lakṣmīsahasra of Veṅkaṭādhvari; Nārāya-ṇīyam of नारायण Bhaṭṭatiri; Dvādaśa-stotra of Madhva; Mūkapañcaśatī of Mūkakavi; and, Ānandasāgarastava of Nīlakaṇṭhadīkṣita.
Apart from this, the epics and the पुराणस् too contain a legion of exquisitely beautiful hymns, some of which like the Viṣṇusahasranāma, the Lalitāsahasra-nāma, the Ādityahṛdaya and the Durgā-saptaśatī have acquired the status of potent mantras. They are extremely popular even now.
SŪKTISĀHITYA
A sūkti or a subhāṣita (= good-saying; wise statement) is like a popular maxim or proverb. It contains the quintessence of the experience of a whole race over several generations. The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे is full of such sayings. They are found interspersed almost in every branch of the literature.
However, several scholars have made serious attempts to bring these sayings together in an organised manner.
The following is the list of some of the better-known compilations: Subhāṣita-ratnakośa of Vidyādhara; Subhāṣitāvalī of Vallabhadeva; Saduktikarṇāmṛta of Śrīdharadāsa; Śārṅgadharapaddhati of Śārṅgadhara; Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra of Kāśīnāthaśarma; Subhāṣitasudhānidhi of सायण and, Subhāṣitanīvī by वेदान्त देशिक.
UPADEŚASĀHITYA
Seeing the abominable deterioration of the moral standards in the society of their times, quite a few poets of the middle ages wrote works in a scintillating style which not only described the things as they were, but also as they should be. Such works may be classified as upadeśasāhitya.
A few such works may be mentioned here: Kuṭṭanīmata of Damodaragupta; Kalāvilāsa of Kṣemendra; Dṛṣṭānta-kalikāśatakam of Kusumadeva; Kali-viḍambana of Nīlakanṭhadīkṣita; Anyokti-muktālatā of Śambhu; and, Bhāvavilāsa of Rudrakavi.
VYĀKARAṆSĀHITYA
The earliest references to Sanskrit grammar are found in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (1.24) and the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (6.4.7). Even though पाणिनि (500 B. C.) was the most brilliant of the grammarians and his Aṣṭādhyāyī eclipsed the earlier works, he does refer to a number of his predecessors such as Āpiśali, Kāśyapa, गार्ग्य, Gālava, Bhāradvāja, Śākaṭāyana and शाकल्य.
(See AṢṬĀDHYĀYĪ and PĀṆINI.)
Many schools of grammar appeared in the post-Pāṇinian period. However, of the six such schools, the one based on the Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa of the Paramāra king भोज (11th century A. D.) became the most extensively used.
Mention may also be made of the following works: Saṅkṣiptasāra of Krama-dīśvara; Mugdhabodha of बोपदेव; Supadmavyākaraṇa of Padmanabha; and, Sārasvatavyākaraṇa of Narendrācārya.
Conclusion
The सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे has been the repository of India’s history, culture, reli-gion, sciences and socio-political values for several millennia. It is in the best interest of Indians to learn it, preserve it and propagate it. It is highly gratifying to note that several countries of the world—both in the east and in the west—are encouraging a study and research of Sanskrit through their centres of learning. It is but meet to declare that India, the motherland of Sanskrit, should in no way lag behind!

Śāntimantras
(‘peace-chants’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
The शान्तिमन्त्रस् are certain hymns chosen from the Vedic literature. They are generally chanted at the beginning and end of Vedic studies, during certain ceremonies called śāntikarmas (propitiatory rites), while doing अभिषेक (bathing the image) in worship and in certain vratas (religious vows and observances).
The number of such mantras as available now is fourteen. Sometimes ten mantras from this are separated and designated as Daśaśāntis.
All the mantras end with the words Oṁ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ.
The word Oṁ when split into its three syllables—a, u and m—gives this meaning: ब्रह्मन् is different from all that we know. It is the very best. It is of the nature of knowledge.
Similarly, the word śāntiḥ when split into śa, anta and i gives the meaning that ब्रह्मन् or God is the acme of knowledge and bliss.
These शान्तिमन्त्रस् may now be dealt with here:
“May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work conjointly with great energy; may our study be vigorous and effective; may we not hate any.”
This is undoubtedly the most popular and oft-repeated śāntimantra.
It belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
The word śāntiḥ is repeated thrice, thereby praying for peace in oneself, in the environment and in the forces that act on both.
It should be noted that the teacher and the disciple are praying together for protection, nourishment and good mutual relationship. Also, that their conjoint study should become effective in their lives.
“May मित्र (the sun) be propitious to us; may वरुण be propitious to us. May Aryamān (a form of the sun) be propitious to us; may इन्द्र and बृहस्पति be propitious to us. May विष्णु of giant steps, be propitious to us.
“Salutation to ब्रह्मा. Salutation to thee, O वायु, Thou indeed art the perceptible ब्रह्मन्. Of thee indeed, the perceptible ब्रह्मन्, will I speak. I will speak of the right. I will speak of the true; may that protect me. May that protect the speaker. Let that protect me. Let that protect the speaker.”
This also is a popular मन्त्र. It forms the very first stanza of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad. The first part of the मन्त्र appears in the Ṛgveda (1.90.9) also.
Indra, मित्र, वरुण, बृहस्पति, विष्णु and Aryamā are the deities presiding over cosmic powers and the corres-ponding functions of the human body. For instance, Aryamā controls the sun and the human eye. The other deities like बृहस्पति who controls speech and intellect, इन्द्र who controls strength of body are also being mentioned and propitiated. If they are pleased, the body-मिन्द् complex will be in good condition and knowledge will be gained effectively.
“May we, O gods, hear what is auspicious with our ears. O ye, who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. May we enjoy the life allotted to us by the gods, offering praise, with our bodies strong of limb.
“May इन्द्र, of great fame, bestow prosperity on us. May पूषन्, the knower of all, bestow prosperity on us. May तार्क्ष्य, of unobstructed path, bestow prosperity on us. May बृहस्पति bestow prosperity on us.”
This śāntimantra belongs to the Atharvaveda.
The very tone and tenor of this मन्त्र shows that the Vedic ṛṣis were not melancholic defeatists but wanted to lead a full life, with all the vigour at their command.
Only when the limbs and the senses are strong, and the duration of life is long, one can achieve great things in life.
For this, the grace of the various cosmic deities is also needed. Hence the prayer to them.
“We pray to God who can destroy our sorrows and grant us happiness. We also pray that the doer of sacrifice gets the very best fruits from the sacrifice. Let us get divine auspiciousness. Let all the human beings also get auspiciousness. In future also, let all our troubles be remedied. Let all human beings attain happiness. Let all our animals attain happiness.”
This śāntimantra is chanted at the beginning and at the end of the famous Puruṣasūkta.
It is used during अभिषेक (bathing the image in ritualistic worship) as also in the सन्ध्या ritual for praying to the Sun in the standing posture (upasthāna).
The first sentence of the text is sometimes interpreted as follows: “I choose to perform (and pray to the fire) the Āruṇaketuka ritual to get rid of all diseases brought about by कर्म, now or in the future.”
“Obeisance to the creator ब्रह्मा. Obeisance to अग्नि (the fire-god). Obeisance to the (Mother) Earth. Obeisance to plants, trees and creepers. I bow down to the (organ of) speech and to the presiding deity of speech. I (also) bow down to विष्णु the all-pervading Cosmic Being.”
This is a prayer for grace, expressing one’s gratefulness not only to God but also to all the powers of nature to which we are always indebted.
Agni or fire (deity) is all important in Vedic rituals. It is he who carries the offerings to the various gods.
The Earth, conceived as our मोथेर्, supports us.
Vegetation sustains our life.
The organ of speech and the power (the presiding deity) behind it help us to acquire knowledge and perform the Vedic rituals.
And of course, God, the all-pervading Cosmic Being, is the very goal of our life.
“Mother Veda invites the gods (for the sacrifice). The Vedic mantras lead us to the performance of sacrifices. May God, the lord of laudatory hymns, give us happiness (when we praise the deities through hymns). May all the gods protect us by speaking to us with words of blessings. O मोथेर् Earth! Do not harm me! I meditate on your benign form. I will compose sweet hymns (in praise of You). I will utter sweet words, I will address others in sweet words. I will offer sweet oblations with sweet words to gods presiding over the rites. To men I will offer pleasant truths sweet to hear, not untruths. So, may gods protect me who does what has been promised. May I shine with fame. May the manes agree to this.”
The first part refers to the Vedic mantras which are used to invite the gods and perform sacrifices.
The word बृहस्पति can refer to ब्रह्मणस्पति, the lord of laudatory hymns.
It may also refer to God, the overseer of Vedic rituals.
‘Viśvedevāḥ’ may also refer to the group of ten deities who are presiding over ṛta or the cosmic law. Their sweet words act as blessings upon us.
The prayer to मोथेर् Earth is because of the possibilities of earthquake, floods, famine and other natural disasters.
Since the gods are propitious towards us, it is our duty to speak sweetly, to praise them sweetly, to think of them with devotion.
It is also necessary to speak sweetly to fellow-human-beings.
So also the proper performance of Vedic rites.
Hence the gods should protect me! And, the manes should appreciate what I am doing, with respect.
“To us, who are the devotees of the Supreme Truth, let the wind blow sweetly. Let the rivers run sweetly. Let the herbs be to us sweet and beneficial. Let there be sweetness in day and night. Let the particles of earth be sweetness-bearing. Let हेअवेन्, our ड़थेर्, be sweet to us. Let the fruit-bearing trees be sweet to us. Let the sun be sweet and beneficial to us. Let the cows be sweetness-bearing to us.”
This मन्त्र forms a part of the famous Trisuparṇamantra (Mahā-नारायण Upaniṣad 38.4-6). Just as सुपर्ण or गरुड protects अमृत (ambrosia) these mantras protect इम्मोर्तलित्य् for us.
These, known as Madhumantras occur in the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (4.2.9) also.
The total idea seems to be that the whole world should be sweet or comfortable for us.
According to one tradition, this मन्त्र is chanted before taking ड़ोओद्.
“Obeisance to the manifested speech. Obeisance to the unmanifested speech. Obeisance to वाचस्पति (the lord of speech). Obeisance to the sages who discovered the Veda- mantras and to those who protected them. Let not these sages who discovered and protected the mantras disown me! Similarly, may I not disown these sages who have discovered and protected the mantras. I will utter pleasant words which are auspicious to all the gods. May the paradise bring us happiness. So also this earth and the whole world. May the sun and the मोओन् bring us happiness. May ब्रह्मा and the Prajāpatis also bring us happiness. I will speak what is good for the animals and for the worlds. I will speak those words which can bring light, honour and austerity. Again, I will speak what is in the वेदस् and what is the truth. To acquire knowledge I will perform this virtuous act. May my virtuous act become a support for human beings and animals. O प्राण and अपान vāyus! Protect me from death. O deities presiding over प्राण and अपान, do not abandon me! I meditate on your benign form. I will compose sweet hymns (in praise of You). I will utter sweet words. I will address others in sweet words. I will offer sweet oblations with sweet words to gods presiding over the rites. To men I will offer pleasant truths sweet to hear, not untruths. So, may gods protect me who does what has been promised. May I shine with fame. May the manes agree to this.”
This long śāntimantra is one of the mantras listed in the Daśaśānti group.
The last part is identical with the last part of the sixth śāntimantra given here (iḍā devahūḥ....).
Homage is being paid to speech in general, to the supervising deities of speech, and to the sages who discovered and transmitted the Vedic mantras.
Brahmā, the creator and the Prajā-patis, the subsidiary lords of further च्रेअतिओन् have been propitiated for our happiness.
The narrator is promising the concerned persons that he will speak words which are true, beneficial to all beings and which are full of light and knowledge.
It ends with a prayer for protection against death.
“May that इन्द्र (or परमेश्वर) who is the greatest in the Vedic hymns, who is of all forms, who has sprung into being from immortal hymns, may he cheer me with intelligence. O God, May I be the possessor of इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
“May my body be very vigorous. May my tongue be exceedingly sweet. May I hear abundantly with my ears. Thou art the sheath of ब्रह्मन्, veiled by intelligence. Protect for me, what I have heard.”
This is a prayer to be repeated by anyone who is desirous of good health and retentive power of मिन्द्. It appears in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.4). It is chanted as a śāntimantra also.
Praṇava or ओङ्कार has been praised here as representing परमेश्वर or God Himself. It is the best symbol for meditation on God.
Since the body, the senses and the मिन्द् are the means for आत्मज्ञान or knowledge of the आत्मन्, a prayer is addressed to God for strengthening them.
The last part of the prayer is for protecting the spiritual wisdom gained by listening to it from the वेदस्.
“May my speech be well-esta-blished in my मिन्द्. May my मिन्द् be well-established in my speech. O self-manifested ब्रह्मन्! Reveal yourself to me. (O speech and मिन्द्!) Bring the meaning and substance of the वेदस् to me. Let not the वेदस् I have heard and learnt abandon me. I will unite the day and the night with my Vedic studies. I will speak ṛta (the right). I will speak सत्य (the truth). May ब्रह्मन् protect me! May It protect my teacher!”
This śāntimantra is allotted to the Ṛgveda. In some texts it forms the last part of the Aitareya Upaniṣad.
Ideas should be expressed through speech after deep thinking, after being convinced that they are सत्य or true.
Since ब्रह्मन् is self-effulgent the prayer addressed to It is for removing the veil of इग्नोरन्चे.
If the वेदस् learnt from the गुरु should be retained in the मिन्द्, the presiding deities of speech and मिन्द् should be propitious. Hence the prayer to them.
‘Uniting day and night’ with Vedic studies means that the study of the वेदस् should be continuous, without any break.
Ṛta is correct understanding based on the study of the scriptures. सत्य is giving expression to it by speech and action.
Protection by ब्रह्मन् is needed both by the teacher (to teach properly) and by the student (to understand correctly).
“He who is rendered holy by the ancient, widespread, sanctifying feet (or by virtuous conduct) crosses over evil deeds and their effects. Having been rendered holy by that naturally pure and purifying feet of the Lord (or conduct), may we overcome our enemies, the sins.”
This मन्त्र occurs in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (1.51) and also in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.12.3).
When a द्विज (the twice-born) takes bath in a river or tank, he should stand in knee-deep water, repeat this मन्त्र and then take bath.
It is repeated at the time of washing the feet of ब्राह्मणस् on special occasions.
In the Mādhva tradition, it is repeated at the time of wearing the mudrās (religions marks) after bath. Here, the word ‘caraṇa’ is taken to mean the सुदर्शन discus of Lord विष्णु.
‘Caraṇa’ represents the feet of Mahāviṣṇu as त्रिविक्रम, from which emerged the river गङ्गा. Hence its remembrance or worship helps us to be purified and to cross over sins.
The word ‘caraṇa’ can also mean ‘śāstrīya-ācaraṇa’, virtuous conduct as ordained by the scriptures. This too helps us to overcome sins.
“May my limbs grow vigorous, my speech, breath, eye, ear as also my strength and all my senses.
“All is the ब्रह्मन् of the उपनिषद्स्. May I never disregard ब्रह्मन्. May ब्रह्मन् never disregard me. May there be no disregarding at all. May there be no disregarding of me.
“Let those truths which are (set forth) in the उपनिषद्स् reside in me (who is) dedicated to the आत्मन् (the Self).”
This śāntimantra belongs to the Sāmaveda. It is chanted at the beginning of Kenopaniṣad and Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
It has three parts. The first part is a prayer for the growth and sustenance of the body in all its aspects. The body being the chief instrument for achieving anything in life, should be kept in excellent condition.
It may be remembered that the śāntimantra ‘bhadraṁ karṇebhiḥ’ (vide 3) also stresses the same idea.
The second part stresses the importance of realising ब्रह्मन् (the Highest Truth) as taught by the उपनिषद्स्. For this, there must be a devotion towards It and favourable response from It. This has, therefore, been stressed.
The last part is an earnest prayer for the firm establishment of the truths taught in the उपनिषद्स्, in one’s own life.
For this, the sādhaka or the aspirant should be devoted to the आत्मन्, same as ब्रह्मन्, as the inner controller in the heart.
“Lead me from the unreal to the Real. Lead me from darkness to light. Lead me from death to इम्मोर्तलित्य्.”
This is a popular and oft-quoted śāntimantra.
Actually, it forms a part of a bigger मन्त्र in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.3.28).
The ‘unreal’ (asat) means ज्ञान (knowledge) and कर्म (actions) which arise according to our lower nature. The ‘real’ means the same, but sanctioned by the scriptures and hence pure.
‘Darkness’ (tamas) means इग्नोरन्चे which covers or hides the truth. ‘Light’ (jyotis) means knowledge which uncovers our real divine nature.
‘Death’ (mṛtyu) is what the unreal and darkness will ultimately lead to. ‘Immortality’ is the final goal of life.
“That (Brahman) is full. This (universe) is full. (From ब्रह्मन् which is) full, (this universe which is) full, has emanated. Taking the full from the full, full itself remains.”
This śāntimantra belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda.
It is quite enigmatic.
According to the Advaita Vedānta, this universe is only a false appearance in ब्रह्मन् due to इग्नोरन्चे, even as a snake is seen in a rope in semi-darkness.
When the rope is seen as rope in full light, it is ‘full’.
When the snake is seen in semidarkness, it is also ‘full’.
After the इल्लुसिओन् of the snake is dispelled by bright light, the rope again appears as ‘full’.
Since ब्रह्मन् is both transcendent and immanent, the birth or the च्रेअतिओन् of the universe does not in any manner affect the integrity of ब्रह्मन्.
This मन्त्र is often used at the end of rites and rituals signifying the completion of the same.
Epilogue
As already indicated in the beginning, each śāntimantra ends with the words ‘(Oṁ) śāntiḥ’, being repeated three times.
The number three may represent:
The three states of consciousness—waking, dream and deep sleep;
the three periods of time—past, present and future;
the three worlds—earth, sky and हेअवेन्;
the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्;
the three Vedas—Ṛg, Yajus and Sāma.
Hence repeating the word ‘śāntiḥ’ three times is said to invoke peace in all these triads.

Śāntis
(‘propitiatory rites’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
It is but natural for human beings to react with the fear of the unknown when eerie unnatural incidents take place. Right from the most ancient times they have also tried to forestall such happenings that might follow, with appropriate propitiatory rites—called शान्तिस् by the Hindu scriptures—in advance. Derived from the root śam (= to appease), the word śānti means a rite that can offset or reduce the evil effects prognosticated by bad omens.
Though this word has not been found in the Ṛgveda in this sense, it does find a prominent place in the Atharvaveda (19.9), the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (6.1.7.7-8) and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (13.10).
Literature on the Śāntis
The literature on the शान्तिस् is quite large. A few of the works may be mentioned here: Kauśikasūtras; Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtras; Matsyapurāṇa; Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa; Agnipurāṇa; Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa; Bṛhatsaṁhitā; Adbhutasāgara; and Śāntikamalākara.
These works have dealt with the शान्तिस् in all their aspects quite extensively.
Adbhuta, उत्पात and Nimitta
The treatises dealing with शान्तिस् generally use three words that prognosticate future events. They are: adbhuta, उत्पात and निमित्त.
Adbhuta refers to any occurrence which has not happened before, or, a total change coming over what has happened earlier.
The adbhutas are divided into seven groups relating to the deities इन्द्र, वरुण, यम, अग्नि, कुबेर, विष्णु and वायु. When some adbhutas take place as related to these deities, certain शान्तिस् are prescribed. For instance, when a rainbow is seen at night, इन्द्र is the god to be appeased. If there is smoke without fire, the deity is अग्नि. The śānti consists in the जप of certain mantras of the Atharvaveda.
The word उत्पात refers to occurrences that portend evil to all. It is the reverse of the usual natural order.
Nimitta, on the other hand, is a prognostic sign which may indicate either an auspicious or an inauspicious event. Generally, it is restricted to the throbbing of a person’s limbs, though it may be used in a wider sense (as उत्पात) also.
Examples of utpātas and nimittas—usually unfavourable—occur plentifully in the Mahābhārata.
The chief utpātas and adbhutas foreboding evil are: terrible द्रेअम्स्; falling of meteors; howling of jackals facing south; sand-showers; earthquakes; solar एच्लिप्से at an unusual time. Vultures sitting on temples; spontaneous fires; halos round the sun or the मोओन्; rain of bloodred water; sudden darkness in the sky; horses shedding tears; rivers flowing in the reverse direction; throbbing of left eye or arm (in men); images of gods trembling, dancing or weeping.
On the other hand, the auspicious signs are: clear and cloudless sky; cool and pleasant wind; fire without smoke; shower of flowers; auspicious birds like herons and peacocks chirping and so on.
Such omens and portents are generally described as occurring at certain important times and events as on the eve of a battle or चोरोनतिओन् or exile of a king and so on.
Śāntis (general)
The पुराणस् like the Matsya and the Agni prescribe different शान्तिस् (of different names) for various purposes. Some of them are: abhayaśānti for a king who wants to conquer others or protect himself against the machinations of the enemies; saumya-śānti for health; vaiṣṇavīśānti to offset the effects of an earthquake or famine; raudrīśānti against epidemics or ghosts; brāhmīśānti against the spread of अथेइस्म्; vāruṇīśānti against drought; kaumārīśānti for the welfare of children; āgneyīśānti to ward off the fear of fire-accidents; yāmyaśānti when there is the fear of accidental death; kauberīśānti when wealth is lost and pārthivīśānti when trees are affected by abnormal conditions.
Some Special Śāntis
GAJAŚĀNTI
Gajaśānti is of two types. The first one, with a simple procedure, is done to restore a sick elephant to health.
The second one described in detail in the Agnipurāṇa (Chapter 291) is aimed at making the royal elephant strong, powerful and inspired so that it protects the king in a battle.
MAHĀŚĀNTI
This is performed to offset the effects of mishaps indicated by such occurrence as the falling of meteors or to facilitate the चोरोनतिओन् of a king or his victory in a battle and so on.
A यज्ञ is performed on a raised platform using mostly mantras from the Ṛgveda. The yajamāna takes a ceremonial bath at the end. Holy water used in the rite is sprinkled over him.
NAVAGRAHAŚĀNTI
Navagrahaśānti, also called नवग्रहमख, is performed to the images of the nine प्लनेत्स् made out of nine different kinds of materials. It is meant to offset the evil effects of the प्लनेत्स्.
The ayutahoma, लक्षहोम and कोटिहोम are its three aspects.
The mantras used are those from the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.
PUṢYASNĀNA
Also known as puṣyābhiṣeka or bārhaspatyasnāna, this rite is reserved for the well-being of kings.
Pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day) associated with the पुष्य नक्षत्र is the best day for the performance of this śānti.
Some of the more important steps of this rite are as follows:
Selecting a suitable spot for the performance of this rite; drawing a मण्डल (geometrical diagram of mystical significance); keeping the various articles on it at appropriate places; होम with special oblations into the fire; sprinkling clarified butter and holy water on the king seated nearby, with mantras; release of prisoners and animals meant for slaughter.
ṢAṢṬYABDAPŪRTIŚĀNTI
Also called उग्ररथशान्ति, it has to be performed by one who has completed sixty years of age. Its aim is to ward off diseases and death and make him live up to a hundred years.
It should be performed in the month of his birth and on the day associated with the नक्षत्र of his birth.
Worship of a small golden image of मृत्यु (= Death; यम), जप of certain Vedic mantras (eg., Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.14.4; Ṛgveda 7.59.12), oblations of cooked ड़ोओद् with appropriate mantras and sprinkling the yajamāna with holy water from the established jars—these are some of the steps involved in the rite.
TRIKAPRASAVAŚĀNTI
The birth of a girl after three successive births of boys or of a boy after three successive births of girls, was supposed to indicate harm to the family like a death or loss of wealth or some other catastrophe. The त्रिकप्रसवशान्ति, to be performed at the earliest on an auspicious day was aimed at offsetting the evil consequences. Worship to the golden images of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, शिव and इन्द्र and होम with mantras from the Ṛgveda (1.22.17) and the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (4.2.8.2) were recommended. Donating a cow apart from the usual दक्षिणा to the chief priest was the last part of the rite.
UDAKAŚĀNTI
This is a comprehensive and popular rite which is practised even now. It is performed for averting the consequences of many evil happenings as also for securing good health and a happy life.
It is an elaborate ritual involving many Vedic mantras, both from the Saṁhitās and the ब्राह्मणस्.
The date for the performance of the śānti is determined by the नक्षत्र (star) of the yajamāna or the performer in his होरोस्चोपे. The chief priest is generally assisted by an even number of ब्राह्मणस्. The śāntijala (propitiatory water) is prepared by him by dipping two कुश grass blades in the kumbha (pot of water) and chanting the appropriate mantras. At the end, the sanctified water is sprinkled over the performer and others (for whose sake it may have been performed).
VĀSTUŚĀNTI
This śānti which is performed even in the modern days, has to be done on the same day or the previous day of गृहप्रवेश (formal entering into a newly-built होउसे, by the yajamāna or owner). The actual day has to be fixed as per the नक्षत्र (birth-star) of the owner. Graha-makha (a rite for propitiating the nine ग्रहस् or प्लनेत्स्), and the usual rites of worship of गणेश are part of this śānti.
A मण्डल (mystical diagram) of 81 squares is drawn and 62 deities are invoked to be present.
Sprinkling of water made holy by appropriate mantras, surrounding the new building thrice with a thread to the accompaniment of suitable mantras from the Ṛgveda (4.4.1-15; 9.1.1-10), digging a pit in the āgneya or the south-east corner and filling it with seven sacred articles and the ceremonial entry into the होउसे by the owner along with his family—these are some of the items of this rite.
Epilogue
Though what cannot be cured will have to be endured, invoking the grace of the Divine will definitely help in reducing, if not eliminating, the effects of unforeseen mishaps. It is this spirit that is at the back of the various शान्तिस् prescribed by the Hindu scriptures. That these rites are still being resorted to is proof enough for their efficacy.
